title: Christian worship, art and liturgy
html:
Christian worship, art and liturgy

John's Christian afterlife is the largest of any figure in this archive except Jesus. It is not evidence about the first century; it is evidence about what communities did with him, and it is unusually well documented in institutions that can be checked.

The calendar

Two feasts carry him: the Nativity of John the Baptist on 24 June (Luke 1 supplies the date six months before Christmas), and the Beheading on 29 August. The Byzantine and Latin calendars, the Orthodox synaxaria and the Roman martyrology all transmit them, and the 24 June feast is old enough that Augustine preaches on its relation to the solstice.

The images

John is one of the most painted figures in Christian art, in three recurring types: the forerunner who points at Christ (the Deesis), the ascetic in camel hair with a reed cross, and the severed head on a platter. The Met's painted copy of the Deesis mosaic from Hagia Sophia, Leonardo's Saint John the Baptist in the Louvre, and Caravaggio's Beheading in Valletta's St John's Co-Cathedral are all documented works in documented collections — useful precisely because the provenance, not the legend, is what can be verified.

The liturgical texts

The Orthodox synaxis and the Latin solemnity present John as the greatest of those born of women and as the forerunner, drawing on Matthew 11:11 and Luke 1:76. The texts are institutional statements about how the churches read him; they are not independent historical testimony, but they show the shape the figure took in worship.
